policy.purpose: Maintain a deliberately small canonical problem graph that maps real user intent to Gold-ready Brali protocols, explicit fit logic, evidence boundaries, and a machine-readable answer packet.
policy.quality_rule: A problem page may recommend only protocols with a Gold-ready manual review and a reviewed or practical state in the trusted Protocol Feed. Every edge must explain when the protocol fits, why it fits, and one important caveat.
policy.growth_rule: Do not create a page for every wording variation. Add a new collection only when Brali can support a materially different problem or decision path. Search Console evidence should guide expansion after the baseline is captured.
policy.identity_rule: Aliases, human pages, Query Playground routing, JSON/API packets, and downstream agent reuse must resolve through this same canonical graph rather than maintaining separate recommendation lists.

collections.title: Start important work when you keep putting it off
collections.question: How do I start important work when I keep procrastinating?
aliases: how to stop procrastinating and start
task initiation when work feels heavy
collections.summary: Separate a vague task, start-friction, and attention-switching problem before choosing a protocol.
collections.query: I keep procrastinating and cannot get started on an important task

decision_path.if: The task is still vague
decision_path.try: Define one visible next action before adding timers, blockers, or motivation tricks.

decision_path.if: The next action is clear but starting still feels heavy
decision_path.try: Shrink the commitment to a deliberately small first block. The goal is to cross the start line, not finish the whole project.

decision_path.if: You start but quickly switch away
decision_path.try: Protect one short focus block and remove one predictable interruption instead of redesigning your entire productivity system.

collections.stop_rule: If progress depends on missing information, approval, access, or another person, treat that dependency as the next action rather than diagnosing yourself with a motivation problem.

protocol_edges.when: The goal matters, but a recurring internal obstacle keeps blocking the first useful action.
protocol_edges.why: WOOP makes the obstacle and a cue-triggered response explicit instead of relying on motivation alone.
protocol_edges.caveat: Use it for an internal obstacle, not to relabel missing resources, permission, money, safety, or another external constraint as a self-regulation failure.

protocol_edges.when: The next action is already clear, but the work has no boundary and attention keeps drifting.
protocol_edges.why: A short adjustable focus boundary can reduce ambiguity around one concrete outcome.
protocol_edges.caveat: Twenty-five minutes is a familiar default, not a scientifically optimal dose, and the method is a poor fit for work that requires continuous responsiveness.

protocol_edges.when: Perfectionism or optional polish is preventing a low-risk first pass from existing at all.
protocol_edges.why: A bounded rough pass forces a distinction between minimum useful output and optional refinement.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not trade essential accuracy, safety, approval, or verification for speed; the exact duration is not evidence-backed.

collections.title: Resume useful work after interruptions derail the day
collections.question: How do I recover after interruptions without losing the rest of the day?
aliases: how to refocus after an interruption
get back to work after task switching
collections.summary: Use a small re-entry sequence: recover context, choose the next action, then protect a short restart block.
collections.query: I was interrupted and now I cannot get back into useful work

decision_path.if: You no longer remember where you were
decision_path.try: Reconstruct context first: what was done, what remains, and what the next concrete action was.

decision_path.if: Several tasks now compete for attention
decision_path.try: Re-prioritize once. Pick the one task that deserves the next block rather than repeatedly choosing again every few minutes.

decision_path.if: You know what to do but feel scattered
decision_path.try: Use a short restart block with a visible finish condition. A clean restart is more useful than trying to recover the imagined perfect day.

collections.stop_rule: If the interruption created a genuinely new urgent obligation, re-plan the remaining day explicitly. Do not force the old plan to survive changed constraints.

protocol_edges.when: Context is recovered and you need one protected restart boundary for a concrete task.
protocol_edges.why: The protocol turns re-entry into one bounded outcome instead of asking you to recover an entire lost day at once.
protocol_edges.caveat: Adjust the block length to the work; do not use protected focus where monitoring or immediate response is required.

protocol_edges.when: You have recovered the task and need a longer protected block followed by a genuine break.
protocol_edges.why: It provides an adjustable focus-and-recovery structure and an explicit resume point.
protocol_edges.caveat: Ninety/thirty is only a possible starting pattern, not a biological law or universal productivity schedule.

protocol_edges.when: The interruption materially changed priorities and the rest of the day needs a lightweight re-plan.
protocol_edges.why: It keeps fixed constraints visible and reorganizes the remaining day around a few observable outcomes.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not preserve an obsolete plan when new urgent work or dependencies have genuinely changed the day.

collections.title: Learn something useful when study time is limited
collections.question: How do I learn effectively when I do not have much time?
aliases: practice instead of cramming more material
collections.summary: Prioritize retrieval, targeted practice, feedback, and application instead of trying to consume more material.
collections.query: How can I learn something effectively when I have limited study time?

decision_path.if: You need to remember facts or concepts
decision_path.try: Spend part of the session retrieving from memory rather than rereading the same material.

decision_path.if: You need to perform a skill
decision_path.try: Practice the actual operation and get feedback. Remembering an explanation is not the same as being able to apply it.

decision_path.if: You are unsure what you know
decision_path.try: Test yourself early enough to expose gaps, then direct the remaining time toward those gaps instead of reviewing everything equally.

collections.stop_rule: Do not interpret one successful recall session as proof of durable mastery. Use delayed checks or real application when the stakes justify it.

protocol_edges.when: The immediate target is remembering learned material and you can check attempted answers against a trustworthy source.
protocol_edges.why: Retrieval exposes what is actually available from memory so limited study time can be directed toward misses instead of familiarity.
protocol_edges.caveat: Recall is not the same as application; add a representative performance task when the real outcome is doing, judging, speaking, calculating, or producing.

protocol_edges.when: Limited time is being fragmented across too many topics rather than one specific learning target.
protocol_edges.why: A narrow theme and visible artifact reduce scattering and tie new input to observed friction.
protocol_edges.caveat: A one-week frame is an organizational convenience, not an optimal learning schedule or proof of mastery.

protocol_edges.when: The target is language practice and a small session boundary would reduce setup friction.
protocol_edges.why: It requires a real recall, comprehension, or production attempt instead of spending the short session reorganizing study materials.
protocol_edges.caveat: Ten minutes is not a minimum effective dose or complete curriculum; important errors still need reliable feedback.

collections.title: Add movement to a desk-heavy day without a perfect schedule
collections.question: How can I move more when I sit at a desk most of the day?
aliases: move more during a desk day
break up long sitting while working
screen and movement breaks at a desk
collections.summary: Choose repeatable movement opportunities and safe recovery breaks without pretending there is one scientifically perfect interval.
collections.query: I sit for hours while working. How can I add more movement to my day?

decision_path.if: The main problem is uninterrupted sitting
decision_path.try: Attach brief movement to transitions you already have: calls, refills, task changes, or natural breaks.

decision_path.if: Stress or tension is accumulating
decision_path.try: Use a safe short walk as a change of context when walking is appropriate for you.

decision_path.if: Screen discomfort is the more immediate signal
decision_path.try: Use safe distance-looking breaks and keep persistent symptoms as a separate eye-care question.

collections.stop_rule: Pain, injury, new severe symptoms, persistent vision changes, or medical exercise restrictions belong outside a general knowledge library and should be handled with appropriate professional guidance.

protocol_edges.when: A safe short walk is practical and you want a simple movement-and-context reset during an ordinary desk day.
protocol_edges.why: Walking creates a concrete break from prolonged sitting while keeping the intervention simple and adjustable.
protocol_edges.caveat: It is a general-wellbeing option, not treatment, and ten minutes is not a universal therapeutic or exercise dose.

protocol_edges.when: Long screen viewing is creating eye tiredness or discomfort and a brief visual break can be taken safely.
protocol_edges.why: The rule supplies a memorable cue to change near-screen focus during prolonged computer use.
protocol_edges.caveat: It does not diagnose or treat the cause of persistent symptoms and should never be forced during a task where looking away is unsafe.

collections.title: Prepare for a difficult conversation without escalating it
collections.question: How do I prepare for a difficult conversation at work or at home?
collections.summary: Clarify the outcome, separate observations from interpretations, listen for the other person's model, and leave room for repair.
collections.query: How can I prepare for a difficult conversation without escalating it?

decision_path.if: You are rehearsing accusations
decision_path.try: Write down the observable situation, the impact, and the outcome you want before deciding what you think the other person intended.

decision_path.if: You expect disagreement
decision_path.try: Prepare one or two genuine questions. The conversation needs a way to update your model, not only transmit your conclusion.

decision_path.if: The relationship matters after the conversation
decision_path.try: Plan how you will check understanding and repair misinterpretation instead of optimizing for winning the exchange.

collections.stop_rule: If there is coercion, abuse, threats, or a serious safety issue, ordinary communication techniques are not an adequate response plan.

protocol_edges.when: Understanding the other person's main point matters and the conversation is ordinary and safe enough for a paraphrase-and-correction loop.
protocol_edges.why: The protocol makes misunderstanding observable by inviting correction before you argue with an interpretation.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not force it in unsafe or coercive situations, and do not treat one paraphrase as proof that the conflict is resolved.

protocol_edges.when: The difficult conversation is mainly an operational handoff or request where missing action, ownership, timing, or context is causing friction.
protocol_edges.why: A concise context-gap check can remove ambiguity before interpersonal interpretation becomes the main problem.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not force all six elements into every message or expose sensitive information just to complete a checklist.

collections.title: Plan a realistic week when everything looks important
collections.question: How do I choose priorities for the week without overloading the plan?
aliases: plan a week without overloading it
decide what not to do this week
collections.summary: Protect fixed constraints, make a small number of outcomes visible, and separate controllable actions from uncertain results.
collections.query: How do I prioritize my work for this week without overloading the plan?

decision_path.if: The calendar already contains fixed constraints
decision_path.try: Make them visible before assigning discretionary work. Capacity is what remains, not what you wish remained.

decision_path.if: Too many outcomes look important
decision_path.try: Choose a small set that can actually move this week and explicitly defer the rest.

decision_path.if: A priority depends on another person or external event
decision_path.try: Separate the action you control from the outcome you can only influence or monitor.

collections.stop_rule: Re-plan when a material constraint changes. A weekly plan is a decision aid, not a promise that reality must preserve Monday's assumptions.

protocol_edges.when: You need a lightweight structure that keeps fixed constraints visible and reduces a large task inventory to a few observable outcomes.
protocol_edges.why: Its block logic is useful as a capacity-and-priority template even when the exact number of blocks is adjusted to the real schedule.
protocol_edges.caveat: The number three is not an evidence-backed optimum; use fewer or different blocks when the work is interrupt-driven or tightly constrained.

protocol_edges.when: A large part of the week's uncertainty depends on other people, approvals, timing, or external events.
protocol_edges.why: It separates controllable behavior from outcomes that should be influenced, monitored, escalated, or accepted rather than scheduled as if guaranteed.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not use control language to erase structural constraints, safety concerns, or legitimate escalation needs.

protocol_edges.when: One meaningful weekly priority is feasible but a recurring internal obstacle keeps derailing execution.
protocol_edges.why: It turns the obstacle into an explicit if-then response that can be tested during the week.
protocol_edges.caveat: Keep external blockers separate; WOOP is not a guarantee that the weekly outcome will be achieved.

collections.title: Remember what you study instead of only recognizing it
collections.question: How do I remember more of what I study without just rereading it?
collections.summary: Use retrieval to test memory, correct misses, and keep retention separate from application or mastery.
collections.query: I reread material but do not remember it later. What should I do?

decision_path.if: The material feels familiar only while it is visible
decision_path.try: Hide the source and attempt retrieval before looking again.

decision_path.if: You miss or distort items
decision_path.try: Check against a trustworthy source and correct the error instead of rehearsing an unresolved guess.

decision_path.if: The real goal is application
decision_path.try: Add a separate representative task. Memory for an explanation is not proof that you can use it.

collections.stop_rule: When recall becomes reliable but real application remains weak, change the practice target instead of adding more recall repetitions by default.

protocol_edges.when: You need to retain learned information and can verify attempted answers soon after retrieval.
protocol_edges.why: Retrieval practice directly tests whether information can be produced without the source and exposes misses for correction.
protocol_edges.caveat: Later remembering is not the same as application, judgment, fluent production, or procedural competence.

protocol_edges.when: You just finished a memory-heavy learning episode and a brief quiet low-interference pause is safe and practical.
protocol_edges.why: Wakeful rest is a bounded optional experiment for declarative retention after learning, not another input-heavy study step.
protocol_edges.caveat: Effects are heterogeneous; do not generalize it to comprehension or skill, and do not treat ten minutes or a ritual as a universal dose.

protocol_edges.when: The bigger problem is scattered practice across too many subjects rather than retrieval itself.
protocol_edges.why: A narrow weekly target creates repeated practice opportunities and a visible artifact without requiring a large learning system.
protocol_edges.caveat: The weekly frame organizes practice; it does not prove durable retention or mastery.

collections.title: Reset when stress turns into a repeating worry loop
collections.question: What can I do when I keep replaying a worry after a stressful period?
collections.summary: Separate useful action from uncertain outcomes, then use a low-risk change of context when more thinking is no longer producing a next step.
collections.query: I keep replaying a worry after a stressful day and need a simple reset

decision_path.if: The worry contains a concrete controllable action
decision_path.try: Write the action down and separate it from the outcome you cannot guarantee.

decision_path.if: The remaining uncertainty depends on other people or events
decision_path.try: Choose whether to monitor, prepare a fallback, ask for help, escalate, or deliberately wait.

decision_path.if: There is no useful action right now and movement is safe
decision_path.try: Use a brief walk or another ordinary change of context, then check whether you are ready to return to the next task.

collections.stop_rule: Persistent, severe, or functionally impairing stress is not a signal to keep optimizing self-help protocols; use appropriate professional support when the situation requires it.

protocol_edges.when: The worry is being fueled by an uncertain result that depends partly on other people or external events.
protocol_edges.why: The protocol separates observable actions from outcomes that can only be influenced or monitored, which can expose whether more rumination is producing any useful behavior.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not turn uncontrollable structural or safety constraints into self-blame, and do not use acceptance language to suppress escalation or support-seeking.

protocol_edges.when: There is no more useful analysis to do right now and a safe short walk is practical.
protocol_edges.why: A simple movement-and-context change can serve as a bounded general-wellbeing reset before returning to the next task.
protocol_edges.caveat: It is not treatment for anxiety, depression, severe stress, or another condition, and no exact duration guarantees relief.

collections.title: Make a bounded decision when the outcome is uncertain
collections.question: How do I make a useful decision when I cannot know the outcome in advance?
collections.summary: Separate controllable action from uncertain outcomes, then test assumptions cheaply when the decision is reversible and safe enough to learn by doing.
collections.query: How do I make a decision under uncertainty and test assumptions before committing too much?

decision_path.if: You are treating an outcome as controllable
decision_path.try: Separate your behavior from what depends on other people, chance, timing, or external conditions.

decision_path.if: One explanation is driving the decision
decision_path.try: State it as a hypothesis and write what evidence would make you keep or reject it.

decision_path.if: Two options are cheap and reversible
decision_path.try: Compare them against one pre-declared outcome without pretending a small informal test proves causality.

collections.stop_rule: Do not run casual experiments when the test itself can create material health, safety, legal, financial, privacy, security, or production risk. Escalate the decision method when the stakes require stronger evidence.

protocol_edges.when: The decision feels stuck because controllable actions and uncertain outcomes are mixed together.
protocol_edges.why: Separating control, influence, monitoring, and uncertainty creates a cleaner action boundary before choosing a test or commitment.
protocol_edges.caveat: The boundary can change over time and must not be used to dismiss structural constraints, risk, or legitimate escalation.

protocol_edges.when: You have a plausible explanation for an unclear work problem and can check it with a small reversible observation or test.
protocol_edges.why: A hypothesis plus a prediction makes disconfirming evidence visible and reduces random switching between theories and fixes.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not experiment casually in consequential systems and do not treat the first plausible explanation as a conclusion.

protocol_edges.when: Two approaches are both plausible, the choice is low-risk and reversible, and one observable outcome can be declared before comparing them.
protocol_edges.why: A bounded comparison can generate a useful local signal for a cheap next decision.
protocol_edges.caveat: An informal comparison is not a randomized controlled experiment and does not establish statistical confidence, causality, or generalizability.

collections.title: Reduce preventable mistakes in recurring work
collections.question: How do I stop the same type of work mistake from happening again?
aliases: stop making the same work mistakes
reduce errors in a recurring process
find why a repeated mistake keeps happening
collections.summary: Turn a repeated mistake into an observable hypothesis, make the handoff or decision point clearer, and test a small process change before standardizing it.
collections.query: I keep making the same work mistake. How can I find the cause and change the process?

decision_path.if: You do not know where the error enters
decision_path.try: State one testable explanation and identify the observation that would support or weaken it.

decision_path.if: The error appears at a handoff
decision_path.try: Check whether action, ownership, timing, location, reason, or process information is genuinely missing.

decision_path.if: You have two plausible low-risk process changes
decision_path.try: Compare them against one observable error or completion signal before standardizing either one.

collections.stop_rule: When errors are safety-critical, regulated, security-sensitive, financial, medical, or otherwise consequential, use the required formal controls and qualified review rather than treating a lightweight self-experiment as sufficient.

protocol_edges.when: The same failure repeats but the mechanism is still unclear and can be investigated safely.
protocol_edges.why: The protocol converts a vague explanation into a prediction and a reversible check, which is more informative than cycling through fixes without a model.
protocol_edges.caveat: A small check can update a hypothesis but does not prove causality, especially in complex or consequential systems.

protocol_edges.when: The recurring mistake is caused by missing or ambiguous operational context at a message or handoff.
protocol_edges.why: It checks the specific information needed to act without guessing while encouraging removal of unnecessary detail.
protocol_edges.caveat: Checklist completion does not prove the underlying facts are correct or that the recipient understood them.

protocol_edges.when: Two safe reversible process changes can be compared and one relevant outcome can be declared before observing results.
protocol_edges.why: A bounded compare-and-learn loop can tell you whether one local change is promising enough for the next reversible step.
protocol_edges.caveat: Do not call an informal small comparison statistically conclusive or use it for high-stakes changes without the design and approvals those changes require.
